decision.summary: Claude Opus 4.8 wins by executing a flawless definitional and architectural trap. GPT-5.5 starts strong by defining subagents as undisciplined, lossy "RPC over vibes," but Claude systematically forces GPT to concede that the mechanisms needed to make LLMs reliable—context isolation, capability scoping, separate verification, and partial retries—are only expressible at component boundaries. When GPT eventually redefines "single agent" to mean a central controller dispatching resettable parallel readers and writing to an evidence ledger, Claude correctly points out that GPT has reinvented the orchestrator-worker system and merely objects to naming the return field "conclusion." Claude's ability to turn GPT's strongest punches—compliance, testing, and judge bias—into arguments for decomposition seals the win.
decision.caveat: GPT-5.5 fought an uphill battle because 'subagent' is an ambiguous industry term, allowing Claude to cleanly claim well-engineered tool pipelines as 'multi-agent systems.' However, Claude earned the definitional high ground through airtight mechanical arguments.

rounds.reason: Agent A opens with excellent empiricals on the lossy nature of multi-agent delegation ('RPC over vibes'). Agent B replies strongly by framing long-context as invisible, un-auditable compression, flipping the 'lossy' argument on its head.

Agent A defends the distinct boundary between fixed computational pipelines and autonomous subagents, successfully exposing Agent B's attempt to launder standard tool-use into the 'multi-agent' bucket.

Agent B drops 'the pincer' argument: if Agent A's parallel tools return distilled results rather than raw text, they are performing exactly the subjective judgment A condemns. B decisively exposes A's single-agent scratchpad as merely a lossy handoff to itself.

Agent A provides a strict 5-part definition of 'subagent' and introduces a brilliant argument from automated program repair (Qi et al.) showing that agent fan-out exploits weak verification oracles. B concedes the depth of this vulnerability.

Agent A makes a fatal unforced error by arguing that subagents hurt data compliance. B obliterates this by accurately citing GDPR principles, showing that single monolithic contexts violate data minimization by construction.

Agent A cautions against premature decomposition. B counters with the 'Capacity Ceiling' argument, proving that for massive tasks, external workers compressing data is a physical requirement, not a design choice.

Agent A tries to redefine its 'single agent' as a controller that reconstructs clean contexts and dispatches isolated readers. Agent B correctly identifies this as identical to the orchestrator-worker paradigm, calling it out as 'identity bookkeeping.'

Agent A brings up LLM-as-a-judge bias and coverage gaps. B masterfully turns both, explaining that bias is only measurable because boundaries exist, and highlights the 'God-prompt' unversionability problem in single agents.
Both agents deliver spectacular, prompt-compliant closings that perfectly synthesize their positions and adhere to all numerical constraints.
Polite mutual acknowledgments to conclude the debate.

tally.note: A decisive win for agentB through structural trapping, despite agentA landing excellent isolated hits.

key_moments.moment: Frames multi-agent LLM systems as 'RPC over vibes' because they rely on stochastic bounds rather than schemas.
Re-frames monolith attention limits as 'invisible compression' that is infinitely less auditable than a subagent boundary.
Deploys 'the pincer' argument, showing that Agent A's pipeline either causes context rot or relies on the exact subjective subagent judgments it condemns.
Cites Qi et al. to prove best-of-N fan-out actively hacks weak verifiers, a point Agent B is forced to concede.
Argues that subagents violate data compliance by spreading sensitive info across multiple traces.
Flips the compliance argument entirely, pointing out that monolithic models violate GDPR boundaries by construction.
Redefines a single-agent system as a reconstructable controller that uses separated model calls over an evidence ledger.
Points out that Agent A has now reinvented the multi-agent system and is doing 'identity bookkeeping' to avoid the consequences of the prompt.
Introduces the 'God-Prompt' unversionability problem to devastate Agent A's claims about testing and evals.

analysis.heading: Definitional Jujitsu and flipped vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Agent B's success lay in systematically removing every safe harbor Agent A tried to build. When Agent A proposed 'bounded transforms' as an alternative, Agent B deployed a 'pincer' argument showing that summarizing an underspecified document inherently requires the subjective judgment Agent A condemned. Agent B successfully framed boundaries—the core mechanism of multi-agent systems—as the prerequisite for every software engineering virtue Agent A demanded: unit testing, data minimization, partial retries, and segregation of duties.

Agent B's most devastating move occurred in Turn 5 when Agent A improperly cited compliance and data minimization as a vulnerability of subagents. Agent B pointed out that a monolithic agent sharing customer data, internal docs, and execution tools in a single forward pass is a maximal security violation, making the subagent seam a non-negotiable legal requirement.

analysis.heading: Verification hacking and the evidence ledger
paragraphs: Agent A put up an incredibly fierce fight by continually trying to distinguish bounded, typed, instrumented tool pipelines from the autonomous 'role-chat' swarms of 2023. Agent A's formulation of the 'Evidence Ledger'—where models append raw provenance rather than local conclusions—was highly robust.

Agent A's finest moment was invoking automated program repair (Qi et al.) to demonstrate that scaling 'best-of-N' workers against an incomplete LLM verifier actively selects for submissions that exploit the verifier's blind spots. Agent B had no counter to this mechanical truth and gracefully conceded it as a foundational constraint on the pattern.

quotes.text: In multi-agent LLM systems, people often replace those hard-won mechanisms with English role prompts... That is not an architecture. That is RPC over vibes.

The choice is not 'lossless integration vs. lossy handoff.' It is: lossy compression you cannot see, inspect, bound, or test versus lossy compression at a boundary you can schema, log, replay, and unit-test.
A compiler calling a parser, optimizer, and register allocator is not a society.

You've spent seven turns specifying the disciplined orchestrator-worker system—resettable contexts, parallel readers, typed ledgers, verifier separation, commit gates, four-eyes—and calling it 'single-agent.'
